title: Junior Analysis Seminar – Oliver Gough (Bath)
desc:
Title

Abstract

I will discuss two results on stable finite-time blow-up for semilinear wave equations with quadratic derivative nonlinearities. In one dimension, both the time-derivative and spatial-derivative nonlinearities admit “generalised self-similar” blow-up solutions. I will begin by briefly reviewing a result on the construction and asymptotic stability of such solutions in the time-derivative case.

The main focus of the talk will be recent joint work with Manuel del Pino and Monica Musso extending this picture to the spatial-derivative nonlinearity in all dimensions n \geq 2. title: SPC Seminar – Plasma – Andrew Lanzrath (MIT)
desc:
Speaker: Andrew Lanzrath (MIT)

Title: Probing light-ion nuclear reactions relevant to astrophysics in high-energy-density plasmas

Abstract: High-quality nuclear data is needed to inform models of big bang and stellar nucleosynthesis. Historically, nuclear reactions have been studied at accelerator facilities where an ion beam impinges upon a cold target. However, in astrophysical environments, these reactions take place in high-energy-density (HED) plasmas. Beam-target fusion reactions in a cold target with bound electrons are not physically comparable to the thermal distributions of reacting ions and free electrons in HED plasmas, which motivated the development of a platform to study nuclear reactions at laser-driven inertial confinement fusion facilities. title: PDEs Seminar – Miles Wheeler (University of Bath)
desc:
Title. Overdetermined problems for the Helmholtz equation

Abstract. We consider overdetermined problems for the Helmholtz equation where one asks for both constant Dirichlet data and constant Neumann data on the entire boundary. It is easy to find explicit radial solutions when the domain is a ball. For zero Neumann data, there is a famous conjecture, attributed to Schiffer, that balls are the only solutions. For zero Dirichlet data, there is a less famous conjecture, attributed to Berenstein, that balls are the only solutions. When both the Dirichlet data and Neumann data can be nonzero, there is an even less famous conjecture, made first by Willms–Gladwell and then by Williams, that balls are the only solutions.

title: David Hand: What’s the Question? Deciding What You Really Want to Know.
desc:
This special event is co-hosted by RSS Data Science and AI and Imperial College London. We are delighted to welcome Professor David Hand OBE, who will deliver a talk based on his latest book, What’s the Question? Deciding What You Really Want to Know :

Before any effective data analysis can be undertaken, we must be clear about the precise question we wish to answer and ensure that it is accurately represented in statistical terms. Ambiguous questions or inappropriate analytical approaches can lead to misleading conclusions and poor decisions. In this talk, Professor Hand will explore this challenge through a range of examples, demonstrating how the most obvious method is not always the most appropriate one, from straightforward problems to complex statistical applications.
